## Overview and grading

### What you'll practice

In this graded assignment,
you'll run a multi-step RNA-seq workflow on the @garrigós2025 data,
from raw reads to transcript counts.
You'll organize it like we discussed in week 10:
with single-step shell scripts that you submit as Slurm batch jobs,
and a Markdown "protocol" with the code to run these scripts in order.
Along the way, you'll quantify gene expression with Salmon,
and you'll summarize the results of all steps in a single MultiQC report.

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Nov 8^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Like for GA3 and GA4,
  you will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an Issue
  in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

::: callout-note
#### Oral examination
As explained in [GA3](GA3.qmd#oral-exam),
each of you will have **one** short oral examination, for one of GA3, GA4, or GA5.
If you haven't had yours yet, it will be for this assignment.
:::

## Instructions

### General

- **Two Markdown files**:
  - Like before, we provide a **template** `README.md` with a section for each question,
    where you add your answers (see "Setting up" below).
    Add commands and their output only where the template asks for them.
  - Separately, you'll build the **protocol** for your workflow in a file `protocol.md`,
    which should contain the final code to run all steps in order,
    like the [protocol example in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#a-protocol-example).
    You don't need to repeat this code in your `README.md`.

- For **each step** where you run a shell script one or more times, you should:
  1. Submit the shell script as one or more batch jobs
  2. Monitor the progress of the job(s)
  3. When they are done, check the Slurm log files and the output files
  4. If you detect failures, try to figure out what went wrong, and rerun
  5. Move the Slurm log files of the successful run(s) into a `logs` dir within
     the script's output dir^[
     The scripts create these `logs` dirs for you.
     This is a small addition that you haven't seen in scripts so far.]

- **Commit** your files to your Git repo as you go along,
  using informative commit messages: commit at least once per Part (A--F).

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The workflow is similar to
[the protocol example in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#a-protocol-example),
but not identical!
To get some genuine practice,
and to avoid copying the wrong things,
we recommend not to copy-paste code from that lecture page.
:::

### Part B: Read QC and trimming

05. Using the code in your protocol, run the FastQC script for all FASTQ files.
    (You'll have to fill in one blank in the loop.)
    How many batch jobs did you submit, and did they all succeed?

06. Take a look at the `trimgalore.sh` script,
    which is similar to the one you worked on in GA4,
    paying particular attention to the arguments it takes.
    Add a loop to your protocol that runs the script once per sample, and run it.

    ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
    #### The TrimGalore output files _(Click to expand)_
    Unlike the TrimGalore script from GA4,
    this script renames the trimmed FASTQ files to the same names as the input files,
    like `S63_R1.fastq.gz`.
    Since TrimGalore runs FastQC on the trimmed files _before_ this renaming,
    the FastQC output files still have names like `S63_R1_val_1_fastqc.html`.
    :::

07. With many Slurm log files, it's easy to miss a count of `0` when scanning
    the output of the `grep -c` command from
    [w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#submit-a-job-for-each-file).
    Since the scripts print a line `# Successfully finished script <script-name>`
    at the very end,
    extend that `grep -c` command so that it **only lists the TrimGalore Slurm log files
    that do _not_ contain this line**.
    (If all jobs succeeded, this command should print nothing:
    to make sure your command works, you can test it on a file that you know
    doesn't contain the line.)

08. The TrimGalore script reserves 8 cores for each job. Use the `seff` command,
    explained on the [self-study Slurm page](../bonus/slurm.qmd#seff-resource-usage-of-a-finished-job),
    to check the resource usage of one of your TrimGalore jobs
    (you can find the job ID in the Slurm log file name).
    What were the CPU efficiency and the memory usage?
    Based on this, would you change the number of cores for this script?

### Part C: Transcript quantification with Salmon

In week 11, the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline first aligned the reads
to the reference **genome** with STAR,
and then used Salmon to quantify gene expression based on those alignments.
Here, you'll use Salmon on its own:
it can also directly map the reads to the reference **transcriptome**,
i.e. to the sequences of all annotated transcripts,
and estimate how many reads came from each transcript.

::: callout-note
#### More about Salmon's mapping approach
This approach is often called **pseudo-alignment**^[
Salmon's documentation calls its default mode "selective alignment",
while "pseudo-alignment" is the term introduced by the similar program kallisto.
In practice, "pseudo-alignment" is commonly used for both,
including by the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline, which can run Salmon in this way
with its `--pseudo_aligner salmon` option.],
because it doesn't produce full read alignments.
Compared to aligning to the genome, it has the following advantages and disadvantages:

- Pseudo-alignment is **much faster** and needs much less memory.
- It doesn't need to be "splice-aware" like STAR:
  since transcript sequences don't contain introns,
  reads from mature mRNAs match them without gaps.
- But you **can only quantify known transcripts**,
  i.e. those in the annotation,
  and you don't get alignment (BAM) files,
  which you would need for other purposes,
  like visualizing alignments or calling variants.
:::

Like with most aligners, Salmon needs an **index** of the reference sequences.
You'll first create this index, and then use it in the quantification step.

09. Take a look at the `salmon_index.sh` script,
    and figure out how you should run it.
    Then, add the code to do so to your protocol, and run it.
    (Only a single index is needed, so you'll run this script just once.)
    When it's done, report how long it took to create the index,
    and how large the index dir is.

10. Now, you can quantify the trimmed reads using the index.
    The script `salmon_quant.sh` does this for _one sample_ at a time,
    and takes 4 arguments:

    1. An R1 FASTQ file
    2. The matching R2 FASTQ file
    3. The Salmon index **dir**
    4. The output dir (the script will create a subdir for each sample in there)

    Read the script, add code to your protocol to run it for all samples, and run it.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Which FASTQ files should you use as input? _(Click to expand)_</summary>

    You should use the _trimmed_ FASTQ files produced by TrimGalore,
    not the raw FASTQ files.
    Therefore, your loop should not loop over the files in `$fastq_dir`.

    </details>

11. Take a look at the main output file for sample `S63`,
    `quant.sf`, and use the [Salmon documentation on its output files](https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/file_formats.html){target="_blank"}
    to answer the following:
    - Of the numeric columns, focus on `NumReads` only:
      what does this column contain?
    - This file has counts for transcripts, not genes.
      But for most analyses, such as a differential expression analysis,
      you'll want counts per gene.
      What extra information would you need to get from transcript counts to gene counts?

12. Which transcripts got the most reads in sample `S63`?
    Write a command that prints the 3 rows of its `quant.sf` file
    with the highest `NumReads` values
    (see the [self-study section on sorting by column](../bonus/shell-data-tools.qmd#sorting-by-column-numerically)).
    Then, look up the FASTA header of the top transcript in the reference transcriptome file,
    and report which gene it belongs to.

14. Salmon reports the **mapping rate**,
    i.e. the percentage of reads that it could assign to a transcript,
    in the file `logs/salmon_quant.log` within each sample's output dir.
    Write a command that prints the mapping rate for all samples at once.
    Which sample has the lowest mapping rate?

### Part D: Summarizing all steps with MultiQC

In GA3, you ran MultiQC on FastQC output only.
But MultiQC recognizes the output of hundreds of bioinformatics programs,
including TrimGalore and Salmon,
and it can summarize all of these in a single report ---
like the report that you saw for the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline in week 11.
So here, you'll run MultiQC once, at the end of the workflow,
on your entire `results` dir.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
MultiQC only recognizes the output of TrimGalore version 2 (which we're using)
since MultiQC version **1.35**.
If your GA3 script used an older version, update its container link.
:::

15. Your `multiqc.sh` script from GA3 was written to be run directly with `bash`.
    Update it so that it is also suitable to be submitted as a batch job,
    following the other scripts for this assignment.
    That is, it should:
    - Have `#SBATCH` lines with the OSC project,
      a descriptive Slurm log file name, and email notification for failed jobs
    - Print the logging statements that the other scripts print
    - Create a `logs` dir in the output dir

    Then, commit the updated script.

16. Add code to your protocol to run MultiQC with `results` as the input dir,
    and `results/multiqc` as the output dir, and run it.
    In the Slurm log, MultiQC reports the number of reports it found for each program.
    For each program, explain why it found this number of reports.

17. Download the MultiQC report, and open it in your browser.
    In the **General Statistics** table at the top,
    which sample has the lowest Salmon mapping rate,
    and does this match your answer to question 14?

### Part F: Bring in genAI

For the last two questions, you'll use Claude Code,
following the same guidelines as in [GA4](GA4.qmd#part-c-bring-in-genai):
use the Manual permission mode and the default model,
start a new conversation for each question,
**export** each conversation to a dir `doc/ai` (e.g. as `q20_protocol-review.txt`),

As in GA4, you are graded on your evaluation of Claude's output,
not on whether Claude happened to give a good answer.

    entire workflow.
    Ask Claude to review **only** your `protocol.md` and the scripts in `scripts/`,

    - Fix the issues that you agree with in your protocol and/or scripts, and commit.

      and describe at least one suggestion that you didn't follow, and why.

21. Ask Claude for a command or a short script that creates a single **summary table**
    for all samples,
    with columns for the sample ID, the number of read pairs before trimming,
    the percentage of read pairs that was kept after trimming,
    and the Salmon mapping rate.
    If it writes a script, save it in `scripts/` and commit it.
    Paste the table into your README.
    Then, check at least 3 of its values against the MultiQC General Statistics table,
    or against your answer to question 14.
    Do the values match (allowing for rounding)?
    If not, figure out which source is wrong, and why.

23. Get a (test) DOI for your repo with Zenodo,
    like we discussed in the [week 11 data management slides](../week11/w11a_data-mgmt.qmd#a-doi-for-your-github-repo-with-zenodo).
    Real Zenodo DOIs are permanent,
    so use the [Zenodo Sandbox](https://sandbox.zenodo.org/){target="_blank"},
    a test copy of Zenodo whose DOIs aren't registered:

    1. In the Sandbox, click "Log in" and choose "GitHub".
    2. In your account menu (top right), go to "GitHub",
       and flip the switch next to your GA5 repo.
       (Don't see it? Click "Sync now".)
    3. On GitHub, open your GA5 repo, click "Create a new release",
       type `v1.0` as the tag ("Create new tag"),
       and click "Publish release".
    4. Back on the Sandbox GitHub page, refresh after a minute,
       and click the DOI badge next to your repo.
    5. Add the DOI to your `README.md` (under question 23), then commit and push.
    6. Flip the switch off again,
       so future releases don't get a DOI.

Finally, on the GitHub page for your repo, create a new **Issue**.

    tag the instructors: GitHub users `kstarr791` and `jelmerp`
